analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to automatically cover newborns for their first month and warn parents of unpaid claims.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the House before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require health insurers and employer plans to automatically cover a newborn for the first 30 days after birth, for any service the plan normally covers. It would then give parents a special window of at least 60 days to formally add the baby to the plan, and require insurers to immediately alert parents if a claim arrives for a baby who is not yet enrolled. The goal is to stop families from getting surprise medical bills for their newborn's care simply because the paperwork to enroll the baby was not finished in time.
analysis.who_benefits: New parents whose babies need medical care in the first weeks of life. Under current rules, a newborn is not automatically enrolled in a parent's health plan, so bills for a NICU stay or a doctor visit can arrive at families who thought the baby was covered. The bill would shift those first-30-day bills to the insurer, give parents a protected 60-day window to enroll the baby without penalty, and force insurers to tell parents right away when a claim comes in for an unenrolled baby — instead of a surprise bill months later.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans and insurers to cover a newborn for the first 30 days after birth for any service the plan otherwise covers, so early-life care is not billed to parents as uncovered.

Creates a special enrollment period of at least 60 days after that first month for parents to add the baby to the plan, protecting families who miss the enrollment paperwork in the chaos of a new birth.

Requires insurers to immediately notify parents when a claim arrives for a newborn who is not enrolled, so families learn about a coverage gap in days rather than through a collection notice months later.
Applies the same rules across employer plans, private insurance, and the tax code provisions governing them, closing gaps families could fall through depending on what kind of coverage they have.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer-sponsored health plans, which would absorb the cost of newborn claims during the automatic 30-day coverage period and run the new notification and enrollment processes. Those costs would flow partly into premiums, and the bills' backers argued the amounts are small because most claims in the first month would have been covered anyway once the baby was enrolled.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The automatic 30-day coverage and notification requirements are a new mandate on insurers and employer plans, and their costs would partly show up in premiums paid by all enrollees, not just families with newborns.

The bill is narrow: it only covers newborns of parents who are already enrolled in a plan, so it does nothing for the children of uninsured parents, and it does not cap what providers can charge during those first 30 days — it just shifts who the bill goes to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted and concrete: it closes a known paperwork trap that produces some of the most distressing medical bills a family can receive, and the insurer cost is limited to one month of otherwise-covered care plus an enrollment window and a notification duty. The main honest objection is that it adds one more coverage mandate to plans and does not address why newborn care can be so expensive in the first place. On balance, the help to families is real and the cost to insurers is modest and specific.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced, one sent it to its health subcommittee, and then nothing more happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on March 18, 2021 with 23 original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Jaime Herrera Beutler, John Katko, Tom Cole, and Brian Fitzpatrick.

The same day, the Speaker's office referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — which meant multiple committees would each have to act on the parts in their jurisdiction before the bill could move.

The Energy and Commerce referral was routed to its Subcommittee on Health, where the bill sat; the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no further action of any kind after March 19, 2021.

The bill gathered 32 cosponsors — 24 Democrats and 8 Republicans — but none of the three committees ever reported it out, and it never reached the House floor before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans are better off, because they never had to take on the automatic 30-day newborn coverage and notification duties. Families who hit the newborn enrollment gap kept bearing the risk of surprise bills for their baby's first-month care.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 32 cosponsors split 24 Democrats and 8 Republicans — and the record shows no one voted against it; the bill died from inaction, not opposition.

industries.note: The bill would require them to pay newborn claims during an automatic 30-day coverage period, run a 60-day special enrollment window, and immediately flag claims for unenrolled babies. Their interest in avoiding the mandate ran directly against new parents' interest in not getting billed for a baby's first-month care.

Self-funded employer plans would be bound by the same ERISA provisions, adding a small administrative and claims cost. The burden is modest, but it is a cost employers currently avoid when a newborn goes unenrolled.
Care delivered in a newborn's first 30 days would be billed to and paid by insurers instead of pursued from families, reducing unpaid bills and collections fights over early-life care.
